title: What a decade of gig work actually pays
summary: On the holiday built to honor American workers, the moving business runs at peak. Data from more than 1.5 million jobs shows what the work pays — and what separates the people who last from the people who don’t.
body_text: Congress made Labor Day a federal holiday in 1894 to honor the American worker. For the people who move Americans and their furniture, it is one of the busiest working weekends of the year. Data from more than 1.5 million completed jobs at Lugg, an on-demand moving and delivery service operating in more than 4,000 U.S. cities, shows Labor Day weekend running 13% to 26% above a typical late-summer weekend in each of the past three years. The holiday Monday itself runs busier than an ordinary Monday in August. The surge is not spread evenly. Boston runs at roughly twice its usual weekend volume , and has in each of the last three years — Los Angeles, the next highest, runs in double digits . The reason is a quirk of the calendar: Labor Day always falls between September 1 and 7, and Boston's residential leases turn over on September 1. The nation's day of rest collides with the city's largest moving day , every single year. Somebody carries all of it. What the work pays, and whether anyone lasts a decade at it, is a harder question than the volume. How long most people actually last Most people who try this work are gone before they learn what it pays at the top. It is hard physical work. Furniture is heavy and awkward, and most of it has to be carried by hand — down stairwells, around tight corners, and out to the truck. Of more than 5,000 movers who took their first job at least five years ago, the median lasted 132 days. Fewer than one in ten were still working five years later. Two of the people who stayed are worth listening to, and they got there by different routes. What actually raises the pay Edgar Teran has been moving furniture professionally in San Francisco for nearly a decade. He spent years in construction before that, decided he wanted something more fulfilling, found the listing online and signed up as a helper — the lowest barrier to entry in the business. No vehicle, no equipment beyond his own supplies, nothing required but a willingness to lift. His very first job was a brand-new white sofa from a CB2 store. He was standing on the loading dock in what he describes as a chaotic scene, looking at a piece of furniture that had to reach the customer in pristine condition. “I was a bit nervous because I didn’t know how I was going to handle it,” he said. “But I had a good partner and we managed it well.” Together they got it into the van, and the delivery went smoothly. That job got him hooked, and he has kept coming back ever since. He was paid as a helper that day, because the van belonged to someone else. Earnings on gig platforms get discussed as though there’s a single rate. In moving there isn’t one. What someone earns depends almost entirely on their role — on what they drive, or whether they drive at all: Role / vehicle Average $/hr, plus tips Moving helper (no vehicle) $18 Pickup truck $28 Cargo van $32–$37 Box truck $42–$47 Those are averages across 22 U.S. markets rather than starting rates, and the spread inside each class comes down to vehicle size — a standard cargo van at the bottom of its band, a sprinter at the top. Tips are uncapped and go entirely to the mover, and a handful clear $1,000 a month from them alone. Lugg publishes a current rate estimator . Edgar crossed to the driver’s side the way many people do before they can do it permanently: he rented. That got him earning at driver rates without the capital a purchase demands, and it let him find out what driving actually netted — what came in, and what went back out — before committing. He bought his own later. Having worked both roles, he knows what the difference actually feels like. “When performing a task, the work is the same for both,” he said, “except that the driver earns a little more due to the vehicle and the responsibility that entails.” The published figures put a helper at $18 an hour and a pickup driver at $28 — a gap of roughly 55%, and considerably wider further up the list. Ten years in, Edgar describes it as a little more. That is because the hourly rate leaves things out. Drivers bring the truck, and mileage and most tolls are reimbursed. The truck is not. Depreciation, insurance, maintenance — or, for anyone still renting, the rental — all come out of the difference. Another path to success The vehicle is the obvious route, and the numbers bear it out: movers still working after five years are considerably more likely to own one than those who stopped in their first year — more than two-thirds of them do. Robert Wilson is one of the exceptions. He spent five years as a helper in Seattle , completed more than 4,500 moves, and never brought a truck to a single one. What he built instead was a reputation and a working knowledge of which jobs are worth taking. “The best jobs are XL deliveries, especially delivering sofas to long-distance destinations,” he said. “A pickup in Seattle and drop-off in Anacortes for an XL delivery. That’s more money.” That is the kind of thing nobody is told and everybody could use. He also has a rule about what not to take: “Don’t accept slots you’re unsure about working.” He starts early and finishes early, because that is the shape of day he wants. The pay table describes one route, and Edgar took it — he acquired a vehicle. Robert stayed on the bottom rung of that list and made the work pay through volume, job selection, and a record that keeps the work coming to him. What a decade teaches Ask either of them what they can do now that they couldn’t at the start, and the answers are unglamorous and specific. “When I started out, I didn’t have much experience with moving and delivery,” Edgar said. “Now I’m an expert — whether it’s navigating staircases, figuring out if items will fit in the truck, or knowing how to work with customers.” What newcomers lack, he says, is exactly that. “The most common issue is the uncertainty about whether the job can be done.” Knowing whether it can be done is the skill. Edgar’s version of it starts with a tape measure. “The first step is to measure the piece,” he said, “then measure the door or staircase and the location where it will be installed. If necessary, we remove the door.” It’s the sort of thing that sounds obvious once someone says it and occurs to almost no one standing in a hallway at the wrong moment. Robert describes something closer to a trained eye. “When moving items, whether it’s sofas, dressers, or anything long, I can see angles within stairwells and tight, shifty hallways that others can’t,” he said. “I know which way to carry the item through the areas.” The expertise turns out to live in the assessment rather than the lifting. Whether the sofa clears the landing. Whether the frame comes off. Which way the dresser turns at the top of the stairs. All of it worked out before anyone has taken hold of anything. Where the money went Robert, who has never owned a truck, puts the outcome in plain terms. “I’ve been able to buy several vehicles, save a substantial amount in my savings account, and now I’m looking to buy property.” Edgar describes something similar in a different register. A decade of the work has paid for his family's standard of living and for goals of his own. He says the work itself has become easier to come by, too — after ten years, he has the experience and the record to get it. He describes the schedule as his own — work, family and friends, all of it synchronized. He spends his time off at home with books and music. When people ask whether they should try it, he tells them it pays, and that it asks for hard work and responsibility in return; he has brought several people into the work himself, and says they have done well. On the decision he made back in 2016, he is unequivocal. “I truly believe it was one of the best things that has happened to me in recent years.” Robert’s version of that advice is shorter. “I’d tell them to join if they’re serious about working. Some jobs will be challenging and some will be easy.” Edgar is an outlier by any measure — the longest-tenured and highest-earning mover on the platform. Moving other people’s furniture has paid him more than $1 million. Some of that is timing. On-demand moving barely existed a decade ago — Lugg was founded in 2014 — so the number of people who could have put ten years into it is small by arithmetic alone. Edgar is close to the ceiling of what is even possible. That is one man’s decade of hard work, not a promise or a forecast. He started out, rented, bought a truck, and was still taking jobs the week this was written. The first Monday in September Nearly ten years after the white sofa, Edgar can look at a piece of furniture and a doorway and know how the job will go before he touches anything. Robert can see the angle a dresser takes at the top of a staircase. Both of them will be working on the first Monday in September — one with a truck he bought, one who never needed one.

title: Launching a million sandboxes per second in constant time
summary: They say that in the future, everyone will have their own sandbox company for 15 minutes. Let's make that simpler, here's exactly how I built our compute platform to handle millions of sandbox...
body_text: They say that in the future, everyone will have their own sandbox company for 15 minutes. Let's make that simpler, here's exactly how I built our compute platform to handle millions of sandbox launches per second in constant time. I hope that you can plug it into Fable/Mythos and get a product out, so that you too can have your own sandbox company. How to build for performance There are two key properties that we're trying to achieve, and they're at odds. First, throughput. We want to be able to launch millions of sandboxes per second. There are two key insights to achieving this property. First, you need a tremendous amount of capacity in order to absorb these sandbox launches. As a result, you cannot have a system which assumes it knows the full state of the world at any given time. Second, you clearly cannot have any point of the system serialize. Two different sandbox launches need to execute completely independently, lock-free. Second, latency. Usually, sandbox platforms trend towards using a bunch of different caches local to the machines running the sandboxes in order to achieve startup times. For our purposes, this is a bad idea because it starts to tightly couple the placement of the sandbox to the performance of that sandbox (i.e. if you have a customer and they run one sandbox, you need to run their next sandbox on the same box in order to get good performance). The key problem with this is that it creates a situation in which your scheduler needs more information in order to function, reducing overall performance. Let's talk about tackling these issues one-by-one. How to launch a million sandboxes per second Let's first look into how we would even design a scheduler to handle a million sandboxes per second. We'll scope this part to literally just getting the sandbox to run on any host, and then tackle latency in the next section (understanding that sandbox locality is explicitly not a property that we want because it will cause bottlenecks). There are two important state management primitives that we'll need for zero bottleneck schedules. First, a database. As you may know, I am partial to Cassandra in all its forms (DynamoDB, BigTable) because I like the property that get O(~1) lookups with IOPs that trivially scale linearly with the size of the cluster that's running Cassandra. The downside here is that we need to be super careful about pre-planning our queries since we won't be able to change them later. Second, storage. If you're not me, you could use @archildata for this, but since we have to avoid circular dependencies in our service, I'm going to just use S3 directly. This gives us scale for free, but the downside with this one is that any request to S3 can't be in the hot path because a 100ms read is going to be too slow for the sandboxes that we want to launch. The purpose of the scheduler is to collect information about how many sandboxes are running on each host at any given time so that, at scheduling time, we can pick which location to use for placement quite quickly. This means that we want to be aggregating the capacity of each host well before we do scheduling, so let's introduce a service for that. Assuming that we are running a cluster of 1 million runtime servers to hold all of these sandboxes, and they report their capacity every 15 seconds, we're looking at close to 70K requests per second. High, but certainly achievable. We want to store each host's capacity inside of our Cassandra so it's easy to look up later when we want to place something on the host. We want to use a primary key for our Cassandra database that has good uniformity over the search space -- so let's assume that we need to map each host's IP address to some kind of random, unique identifier like a UUID. We should have our capacity aggregation service own uploading this mapping into something like S3. Assuming that we have 64-bit server identifiers and 32-bit IP addresses, this mapping should be on the order of 12 MB. Again, large, but certainly something that we can do -- and we can split it into different pages if we need to. We'll have our Capacity Aggregation service also be responsible for new host registration, so we just add a host to the fleet, it starts reporting capacity, and our service add its to Cassandra. As a result, we need one of our "Capacity service" hosts (some kind of leader election will have to happen) to be responsible for periodically scanning Cassandra and putting the mapping of UUID to IP addresses into S3, but because host turnover is slow, this can happen on the order of minutes. Similarly, we don't have to immediately detect dead hosts instantly so long as we have a low probability of selecting them, so let's assume that there's some slow process in this server that scans our Cassandra table to look for servers which haven't sent capacity in a while and removes them. The great part about centralizing this into a single service is that it can also be responsible for a bunch of other functions we might want, like quiescing a host that's alive so that we can deploy to it without disrupting customer workloads. Let's look at the actual host selection path: People give microservices a bad rap, but it's a super simple way to build something that will scale forever, and this is probably less than 10K lines of code (not that we care about that anymore). Our API service will be, in the background, periodically (O(minutes)) refreshing the list of hosts from our mapping file stored in S3. This will give us a slightly out-of-date view of which hosts are alive (you will note that "slightly out of date" is a common theme). When a customer requests a sandbox, we can now select from this list with uniform randomness. We will pick 2 at random (or whatever "best-of-X" you prefer), and then query Cassandra for both of those hosts (let's assume ~10ms) to get their slightly-out-of-date capacity information. We'll select the host with the most capacity and attempt to put the sandbox on that host. If this fails (either for capacity reasons or for health reasons), we will report the failure to the capacity service to take the appropriate action (either update or remove the host). If it fails, we'll try the other host we selected, or pick again. This gives us a 10ms scheduling p50, and a slightly higher p99 depending on how frequently we pick bad hosts. Depending on your goals as a platform, you can tune the probability of picking a bad host by: selecting more or fewer hosts to query, updating the capacity information more or less frequently, and potentially sandbagging capacity by always reporting values that are lower than the actual host capacity. There's nothing in this path that has any kind of locking out, so we can now launch one million sandboxes per second in around 10ms. What's next? How to launch sandboxes in constant time The next usual challenge here is how we do this in a way that doesn't have terrible cold-start latencies depending on the placement. We just built a placement service that doesn't consider any constraints on the host that we pick, so we need to make sure that we can get the sandbox up in the same amount of time no matter what host it lands on. Actually booting the sandbox usually isn't a problem because you can get constant time trivially by just always booting them. On the other end of the spectrum, you can do what @archildata does and have every sandbox that the platform could run already prebooted, and lock customers into a few different shapes of choices (which we can signal to the schedule by reporting more complex capacity information in our reports). The reader can decide which way they want go here. In fact, the usual problem with a sandbox platform is actually the image that the user wants to use on their host. Users aren't very good at building their workloads around the constraints of the system, so as much as we all wish that all of our container images were like 10 MB, it turns out that most container images in production are more on the order of 500 MB to 2 GB. Now, this poses a problem. The usual way that container platforms are built is that the user will "prepare" or upload their container image into some kind of a registry. This is usually S3-backed storage. When they launch the container on the host, then the host will actually pull down the image to a local cache. This makes warm startups (scheduling the same container on the same host) quite fast (the image is already there), but it makes cold starts terrible. If you download from S3 naively (80 MB/s) it can take nearly 25 seconds to get a 2 GB image downloaded to the runtime host. This is not great for consistency when a warm startup can do this in 0 seconds. As a result, many systems end up trying to do image-aware placement to maximize the chances that the user's container lands on a host that has already done this download. This, of course, introduces bottlenecks into the placement process which ends up limiting the speed at which the system can launch containers. Worse, most container launches don't actually need to read 100% of the image bytes to actually startup, so a lazy-loading approach could significantly improve these cold-start times. Lucky for us, in 2026, we can use high-speed file storage (like @archildata ) to just host the images for us, because they provide online access to the data from all of these hosts without needing a download step. In this world, we put all of the container images that customers want (via a "preparation step") onto a file system that they already own. Unlike the capacity management (which is an issue for operating the sandbox service) we do get to use Archil for image storage because we think of those images as belonging to each user, which means that they can use the Archil disks that they already have to hold the images. Because this is disaggregated storage, all 1 million hosts in the service are able to access the data at the same speed and read only the bytes they need. Even though the sandboxes are already booted, we can easily tell Linux to swap into the container namespace from the disaggregated storage system as part of the "launch" process. This means that we now can launch any container, on any host, in the same amount of time, regardless of the image size that the container wants to use. Let's look at the entire architecture diagram. As you probably realize, this isn't actually a complex thing to build. I think that the core reason why "scheduling" gets a bad rap about being difficult is for a lot of random reasons: I think that people are used to thinking about using Kubernetes for problems, which isn't singularly designed for the task of placement and scaling containers I suspect that many system designs rely on relational databases that are more challenging to scale, out of the box, which run into issues I believe that many schedulers being built today (especially given the race to build sandboxes) are likely trying to do fully-consistent capacity management, which isn't possible at high levels of scale People don't immediately reach for online shared storage like @archildata , instead opting to try to upload+download things from places like S3 (slow) If you want any of the code to prepare Docker images into an efficient format to store on Archil (or other file storage) or the code to "launch" that Docker image (w/o installing Docker), then please DM me and I'll shoot it your way. Anyway, I hope that you go off and build a sandbox company with this blueprint. Obviously, there's lots more that has to happen besides just getting a container running on a host using a Docker image, but I think that everything else should be relatively straightforward for you and Fable. Please let me know if you feed this to your Claude and something pops out!

body_text: NEW YORK, Aug. 06, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) — Resolute Holdings Management, Inc. (“Resolute Holdings”) (NYSE: RHLD), an operating management company responsible for providing management services to the operating businesses of GPGI, Inc. (“GPGI”) (NYSE: GPGI), today reported financial results for its fiscal second quarter ended June 30, 2026. Resolute Holdings reported second quarter earnings per share attributable to common stockholders of $(1.53) compared to ($0.07) in the prior year and Non-GAAP Fee-Related Earnings per share of $0.69 compared to $0.08 in the prior year. The increase in Non-GAAP profitability was driven by the higher fee stream as a result of the execution of the management agreement with Husky Holdings LLC (“Husky Holdings”) in January 2026, along with organic growth in fees from the CompoSecure management agreement. During the second quarter and through the end of July, the company repurchased $50.0 million in common shares in open market purchases and has reduced its shares outstanding by approximately 8.3% since the spin-off. As a result of the spin-off from GPGI and execution of the management agreement with GPGI Holdings, L.L.C. (“GPGI Holdings”), Resolute Holdings is required to consolidate the financial results of GPGI Holdings (and its subsidiaries, including Husky Holdings) in accordance with U.S. GAAP. This presentation of financial results does not represent the underlying economics or the positive attributes of Resolute Holdings’ standalone business model, which consist of recurring, long-duration management fees and a relatively fixed expense base. The results of the Resolute Holdings standalone business and associated Non-GAAP Fee-Related Earnings calculation are included below to provide a clear picture of the economic performance of the business directly attributable to shareholders of RHLD. This release includes such results presented in accordance with U.S. GAAP, as well as certain Non-GAAP measures, including Fee-Related Earnings. See “Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures” below. body_text: President Donald Trump’s long-standing preference for McDonald’s has once again drawn attention after Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. explained why the president reportedly turns to major fast-food chains when traveling. According to Kennedy, Trump’s choice is not simply about taste or convenience. He said Trump prefers familiar national restaurant chains while on the road because he is concerned about getting food poisoning from unfamiliar establishments. The comments have renewed interest in Donald Trump’s diet, McDonald’s, food safety, and the Make America Healthy Again initiative , particularly because Kennedy is leading the federal government’s health agenda. RFK Jr. Explains Trump’s McDonald’s Habit Kennedy discussed Trump’s eating habits during an appearance on the Net Positive podcast published in August 2026. He said Trump generally enjoys high-quality food but changes his approach when traveling. Kennedy described seeing large quantities of McDonald’s food aboard the presidential aircraft and said Trump has confidence in national chains because he believes their standardized operations provide a more predictable food experience. The explanation adds another dimension to Trump’s well-known relationship with McDonald’s. The president has spoken publicly for years about his preference for the restaurant, while photographs and public appearances have frequently shown him with fast food. Trump’s choice has often been associated with convenience and familiarity. Kennedy’s latest comments suggest that food safety concerns may also influence those decisions. That distinction is important. The claim is about Trump’s personal reasoning, rather than evidence that McDonald’s is universally safer than independent restaurants. Food safety can vary between individual restaurants, food suppliers, preparation practices, and local conditions. Trump’s Diet Changes When He Is at Home Kennedy also drew a contrast between Trump’s meals while traveling and what he eats at the White House or Mar-a-Lago. According to Kennedy, Trump has access to fresh food, chefs, and locally sourced produce when he is at his regular residences. In those settings, Kennedy characterized the president’s diet as considerably better than what he consumes while traveling. The contrast helps explain why Kennedy’s comments should not necessarily be interpreted as saying Trump eats fast food for every meal. Instead, the description suggests that travel creates a different set of priorities. Trump reportedly values consistency and familiarity when he is away from his usual kitchens and food suppliers. For a president who spends substantial time traveling for political events, diplomatic meetings and official duties, food logistics can also be more complicated than they are for an ordinary traveler. Trump’s Long History With McDonald’s Donald Trump’s McDonald’s habit is hardly new. During his 2024 presidential campaign, Trump made headlines when he worked behind the counter at a McDonald’s restaurant in Pennsylvania. His campaign appearances have also frequently incorporated fast food, reinforcing his public image as a longtime fan of the chain. Trump has previously pointed to consistency and cleanliness as reasons for his preference. His affinity for McDonald’s has become a recognizable part of his public persona, much like his well-known preference for Diet Coke. Kennedy has previously discussed Trump’s consumption of fast food, sweets and Diet Coke. Earlier comments also highlighted a distinction between Trump’s travel habits and his meals at the White House and Mar-a-Lago. The latest remarks therefore fit into a broader pattern Kennedy has described rather than representing a completely new claim about the president’s eating habits. Why the Comments Matter for the MAHA Agenda Kennedy’s comments are particularly notable because of his leadership of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, initiative . The administration has emphasized reducing reliance on highly processed foods and encouraging Americans to consume what it describes as “real food.” The federal health agenda has also focused heavily on chronic disease, nutrition, food ingredients and the American food supply. The official HHS MAHA website says the initiative is aimed at addressing what the department describes as the country’s chronic disease crisis. HHS currently cites several health statistics, including its claim that 40 percent of the U.S. population is dangerously close to becoming diabetic or prediabetic. The department also highlights efforts involving food policy, nutrition and artificial food dyes. Its MAHA information page says 40 percent of the U.S. food and beverage industry has committed to removing artificial dyes, while the department also reports that multiple states have adopted policies restricting certain food purchases through SNAP. That creates an obvious point of public interest when the health secretary discusses the eating habits of the president he serves. Kennedy, however, has indicated that he does not intend to act as a personal “scold” toward Trump. His comments have generally presented the president’s food choices as a personal matter while emphasizing the broader policy goal of improving Americans’ diets. Food Safety Versus Nutrition The Trump-McDonald’s discussion also raises an interesting distinction between food safety and nutritional quality . A restaurant meal can be prepared safely while still being high in calories, sodium, saturated fat or other nutrients that consumers may want to limit depending on their individual dietary needs. Likewise, choosing a familiar chain because of concerns about food poisoning does not automatically make every menu item a healthy choice. Food safety involves preventing contamination and illness. Nutrition involves the overall composition of a person’s diet. The two issues overlap, but they are not the same. For travelers, the practical lesson is that familiarity may influence restaurant choices, but consumers should still consider balanced meals, portion sizes and dietary variety. Kennedy Promotes Cooking at Home During his podcast appearance, Kennedy also discussed the importance of preparing food at home. He argued that Americans should regain confidence in basic cooking and make healthier meals without spending excessive amounts of money. That message aligns with the broader MAHA emphasis on changing eating habits rather than focusing exclusively on individual medical treatments. The administration has increasingly framed nutrition as an important part of addressing chronic disease. HHS says its MAHA initiative is intended to identify and address root causes of chronic health problems. Whether those policies ultimately produce measurable improvements in national health remains an ongoing subject of debate. What RFK Jr.’s Comments Reveal About Trump’s Diet Kennedy’s latest comments offer a relatively simple explanation for one of Trump’s most recognizable eating habits. When traveling, Trump reportedly prefers national chains such as McDonald’s because he trusts their consistency and worries about becoming sick from unfamiliar food. At the White House and Mar-a-Lago, Kennedy says the president has access to fresher foods and locally sourced ingredients. The story is therefore less about one fast-food restaurant and more about the complicated relationship between food safety, convenience, personal preference and nutrition . Trump’s affection for McDonald’s has been public for decades, but Kennedy’s explanation provides additional insight into why the president continues to choose the chain while traveling. It also highlights an unusual contrast within the administration. The president is known for fast food and Diet Coke, while his health secretary is leading an initiative focused on improving American nutrition and reducing chronic disease. For now, Kennedy says he is not trying to police Trump’s personal menu. Instead, his focus remains on the broader MAHA effort to encourage Americans to rethink what they eat and how their food is produced. Sources: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Make America Healthy Again initiative; ABC News reporting on RFK Jr.’s comments; Washington Examiner reporting on Trump’s dietary habits. Disclaimer: Statements attributed to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. or other individuals are presented as their claims or descriptions and should not be interpreted as independent verification. The article is for general informational purposes and is not medical or dietary advice. Readers should consult qualified health professionals for individual nutrition or health concerns.

title: 25 Side Income Sources in India That Actually Pay (2026)
summary: Where to start each one, and what it actually pays.
body_text: Most side income sources pay in one of two ways: for your hours, or for an outcome. Hourly work has a hard ceiling, because there are only so many evenings in a week. Outcome-based work does not, which is why selling financial products sits at the top of this list and survey apps sit near the bottom. Every entry below carries the same three things: what it is, where to actually start it, and what it typically pays. Key Takeaways Selling financial products pays per approved application rather than per hour, with commissions up to Rs 2,000 on a single approved credit card. Refer and earn is the easiest thing to start, but most app referral programmes pay in coins, vouchers or credit rather than cash. Freelancing, tutoring and design pay well but stop paying the moment you stop working. Treat them as income, not as a business. If you have a job, read your employment contract before starting anything. Some employers require written permission for outside work. Anything that asks you to pay a joining fee, buy a kit or invest first is not a side income source. It is a purchase. Table of contents What Counts as a Side Income Source? How to Choose a Second Source of Income Commission-Based Sources (1 to 2) Phone and Laptop Sources (3 to 10) Skill-Based Sources (11 to 17) Time and Asset Based Sources (18 to 25) Which Side Income Sources Work Alongside a Job? Which Side Income Sources Suit Students? Extra Income Sources Worth Avoiding What You Can Realistically Earn What Counts as a Side Income Source? A side income source is any repeatable way of earning money outside your main job or business. Three kinds exist, and the difference decides your ceiling. Time-for-money. Freelancing, tutoring, driving, delivery. Reliable, immediate, and capped by the hours you have. Outcome-for-money. Commission on a sale, a completed application, a closed deal. Pays nothing when it fails and pays properly when it works, and one good month does not require twice the hours. Asset-for-money. Renting a room, a bike or camera gear, or earning interest on savings. Needs something you already own, then runs quietly. The same evening spent two ways. Only one of them scales. Most lists mix all three and rank them by how exciting they sound. This one ranks by what an hour spent is actually worth, so the order below won't match what you've read elsewhere. How to Choose a Second Source of Income Four filters, applied in this order, remove about twenty of the twenty-five for any given person. Capital needed. If it asks for money upfront, it is a business, not a side income. Start with what costs nothing. Time it fits into. Evenings and weekends, or gaps in the day? A tiffin service needs mornings. Sharing a product link needs four minutes. Skill you already have. The fastest starts use something you can already do, even if that skill is simply being trusted by people around you. Where the ceiling sits. Ask what this pays if it goes really well for a year. Some of these top out at pocket money by design. Run those four filters honestly and the list usually shortens to two or three real options. Start one, not three, because three at once is how people end up with none. About the pay ranges below. Each entry carries a typical Indian range for 2026, based on what these platforms and local markets commonly pay. Ranges move with city, skill, demand and season, and beginners often start below the lower end. None of them is a promise. GroMo commissions are the exception, because those come from the app's own catalogue and can be checked live before you quote them. Commission-Based Sources (1 to 2) 1. Selling financial products with GroMo GroMo is an Indian financial products distribution app. Partners recommend credit cards, savings accounts, demat accounts, loans and credit lines from a single catalogue, and earn a commission when an application is approved. Where to start. Install the GroMo app , sign up, register as a partner, and share one product with someone it suits. Your PAN comes in at withdrawal, once a sale is confirmed. What it pays. Per approved application, by product category: Product category Pays up to per approved application Credit Card Rs 2,000 Investment Rs 1,000 Savings Account Rs 750 Personal Loan Rs 500 Demat Account Rs 400 Credit Line Rs 150 Please note. Every figure above is a maximum rather than a flat fee, and comes from the app (GroMo product catalogue). Commissions are campaign-linked, so they move and can change without notice. The rate showing on the product card when you share it is the one you get paid. One approved application, by product category. The honest catch. This needs a conversation. If you can't picture explaining a credit card to a cousin, a freelance skill will suit you better. Approvals are decided by banks, so some months are quiet. Best for anyone whose friends and family already ask them for money advice. 2. Refer and earn Referral programmes pay you for bringing a new user to an app. Every category runs one, and the payouts vary more widely than in any other entry on this list. Where to start. GroMo's referral programme sits inside the app. Beyond it, broker apps such as Upstox, Groww and Angel One run their own schemes, payment apps like PhonePe and Paytm run smaller ones, and shopping apps such as Meesho and Amazon pay for installs and first orders. What it pays. Financial referrals are the serious end, usually a few hundred to a couple of thousand rupees per successful referral, paid as cash to a bank account. Payment and shopping apps typically pay tens of rupees, often as wallet credit or a scratch card. Task, game and survey apps pay in coins worth a fraction of a rupee. The question to ask any programme. Does it pay cash to a bank, and does it pay when your friend signs up or only after they transact? Programmes that pay only once your referral spends money are worth far less than they look. Best for absolutely everyone as a starting point, and almost nobody as a whole plan. Phone and Laptop Sources (3 to 10) 3. Freelance writing and editing Blogs, product descriptions, newsletters, resumes and case studies, written to a brief. Where to start. Upwork, Fiverr, Contra and Internshala for listed work, plus direct outreach on LinkedIn to marketing managers at small companies. Regional-language writing is undersupplied. What it pays. Roughly Rs 500 to Rs 2,000 for a standard blog article at the start, rising past Rs 3,000 once you have a portfolio and a niche. Rates rise fast with a niche. Pick one. Best for anyone who writes clearly and hits deadlines without being chased. 4. Graphic design and template selling Posters for local businesses, wedding invitations, social media kits, and templates that sell repeatedly. Where to start. Fiverr and Behance for clients, Canva's creator programme and Etsy for templates, and your neighbourhood market for the fastest first customer. What it pays. About Rs 300 to Rs 1,500 for a single poster or invitation, and Rs 5,000 to Rs 25,000 for a small brand identity package. Templates keep selling after you've made them once. Best for people with a design eye who would rather make things than talk to people. 5. Online tutoring School subjects, spoken English or competitive exam prep, taught one to one or in small batches. Where to start. Vedantu, Chegg India and Superprof for platform work, and local parent WhatsApp groups for direct students, who pay more because no platform takes a cut. What it pays. Around Rs 200 to Rs 800 an hour, with maths, science and exam coaching at the top of that range. Direct students pay more. Always. Best for anyone with a subject they know well and the patience to explain it twice. 6. YouTube A channel that compounds slowly and keeps paying long after a video is made. Where to start. YouTube itself, with monetisation unlocked after the platform's subscriber and watch-hour thresholds. Regional-language explainer channels face far less competition than English ones. What it pays. Nothing for the first several months. Once monetised, Indian channels commonly see a few tens to a couple of hundred rupees per thousand views, and brand deals usually pay more than the ad revenue does. It's the slowest thing here. It's also the one that keeps paying. Best for people willing to publish for six months before judging it. What the phone and laptop routes typically pay in 2026. 7. Instagram content for brands Reels, photos and captions made for businesses that have no time to produce their own. Where to start. Local businesses first, gyms, cafes, salons and boutiques, then creator marketplaces once you have samples to show. What it pays. Roughly Rs 1,000 to Rs 10,000 per reel for a small creator working with local brands, and monthly retainers pay better than one-off posts. Local brands are the easy first yes. Best for anyone comfortable on camera or good at editing on a phone. 8. Affiliate marketing Commission for products bought through your link, across retail, software and financial products. Where to start. Amazon Associates, Flipkart Affiliate and EarnKaro for retail, and financial product platforms for higher-value categories. What it pays. Retail links pay a small share of each sale, often only a few rupees an order, which is why volume decides everything. Financial and software products pay far more per conversion. No audience, no affiliate income. That's the whole rule. Best for people who already have an audience that trusts their recommendations. 9. Blogging Your own site, earning from ads and affiliate links, built for search traffic. Where to start. A domain, hosting and WordPress, one narrow topic you can cover better than anyone else, and Google AdSense once traffic exists. What it pays. Nothing for six to twelve months. A blog with steady search traffic can earn a few thousand rupees a month from ads, and considerably more from affiliate placements. Payback is slow. Compounding is real. Best for patient people who enjoy writing and are willing to learn SEO. 10. Reselling on WhatsApp Sourcing from wholesale apps and selling into your own network without holding stock. Where to start. Meesho, GlowRoad and Shop101 for catalogues, and your existing WhatsApp and Facebook groups for customers. What it pays. A margin you set yourself, commonly Rs 50 to Rs 300 an item, so earnings follow order volume rather than effort per sale. Returns eat the margin, so check them first. Best for people with an active network and time for follow-up messaging. The order here follows what an hour buys, not how new the idea is. Skill-Based Sources (11 to 17) 11. Web and app development Small business websites, landing pages, fixes and integrations, built on evenings and weekends. Where to start. Upwork and Toptal for remote clients, local business networks for direct work, and agencies that outsource overflow. What it pays. Around Rs 8,000 to Rs 50,000 for a small business website, and the highest hourly rate on this list once you have references. Nothing else here pays this well per evening. Best for developers who want maximum return per hour. 12. Voice-over and dubbing Ads, explainer videos, e-learning modules and audiobooks, recorded from a quiet room. Where to start. Voices.com and Fiverr for international work, and Indian dubbing studios and ad agencies for regional-language jobs. What it pays. Roughly Rs 500 to Rs 5,000 per short project at the start, with regional accents and languages paying more than neutral English. Best for people with a clear voice and the discipline to do retakes. 13. Transcription and captioning Turning audio into text and adding captions to video. Unglamorous, and always available. Where to start. Rev, GoTranscript and TranscribeMe for English, and Indian media houses for regional-language work. What it pays. Roughly Rs 20 to Rs 60 per audio minute, so typing speed and accuracy decide your hourly rate. You won't speak to a single client. Some people want exactly that. Best for fast typists who want work that needs no client conversation. 14. Translation English into Hindi, Marathi, Tamil or Bengali and back, for brands localising content. Where to start. ProZ and Upwork for professional work, Indian content agencies for volume, and app localisation projects for repeat clients. What it pays. Commonly Rs 1 to Rs 3 a word, with technical, legal and medical translation at the higher end. Conversational isn't enough here. Best for anyone genuinely fluent in two languages, not just conversational. 15. Virtual assistant work Inbox, scheduling, research, data and coordination work for founders and small agencies. Where to start. Upwork and Wishup for structured roles, and founder communities on LinkedIn for direct hires. What it pays. Roughly Rs 8,000 to Rs 25,000 a month for part-time hours, with international clients paying substantially more. Best for organised people who like closing loops for somebody else. 16. Photography and videography Weddings, events and product shoots, priced by the day. Where to start. Second-shooter work with an established photographer first, then WedMeGood and local wedding planners once you have a portfolio. What it pays. Around Rs 5,000 to Rs 25,000 per event day as a second shooter or on small shoots, and more once you own the client relationship. Your weekends go first. Be honest about that. Best for people who already own a camera and can give up weekends. 17. Teaching a craft Yoga, music, dance, fitness or cooking, taught in small batches online or in person. Where to start. Your own building and neighbourhood groups, a local studio that rents slots by the hour, and Instagram to fill batches. What it pays. Roughly Rs 1,500 to Rs 4,000 per student a month for a regular batch, so eight students is a real second income. Eight students changes a month. Best for anyone with a skill people already ask them to teach. Apply the four filters before you start anything. Time and Asset Based Sources (18 to 25) 18. Ride-hailing and delivery Driving or delivering in hours you can spare. Immediate money, hard ceiling. Where to start. Uber, Ola and Rapido for rides, Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto and Blinkit for delivery. Onboarding takes a few days. What it pays. Roughly Rs 10,000 to Rs 20,000 a month for genuine part-time hours, before fuel and maintenance, which are the costs most people forget to subtract. Money arrives fast. It also stops the day you do. Best for people with a vehicle and fixed free hours who want money this week. 19. Renting out a room The largest asset most families own, and the most underused one. Where to start. Airbnb for short stays, NoBroker and Nestaway for long-term tenants, and your own society noticeboard for the fastest match. What it pays. Roughly Rs 5,000 to Rs 20,000 a month depending on the city and whether the room is furnished. Best for households with a genuinely spare room and no objection to sharing space. 20. Renting out equipment Camera gear, a bike, power tools or party equipment, earning while you are at work. Where to start. RentSher and local Facebook groups, plus photography WhatsApp groups where gear rental is routine. What it pays. Around Rs 500 to Rs 3,000 a day for camera bodies and lenses, less for tools, and it only works if you already own the item. Best for people whose expensive hobby equipment sits idle most weeks. What the time and asset routes typically pay in 2026. 21. Tiffin service Home-cooked meals for regular customers, billed monthly. Steady, and demanding every single morning. Where to start. Nearby offices, PG accommodations and hostels, then delivery apps once the kitchen routine is proven. What it pays. Roughly Rs 2,500 to Rs 4,000 per customer a month, so fifteen regulars is a serious business rather than a side income. Every morning. No exceptions. Best for people who cook well and can commit to mornings without exception. 22. Home baking and festival orders Cakes, cookies and hampers, peaking around festivals and birthdays. Where to start. Instagram for showing the work, WhatsApp status for taking orders, and your building group for the first customers. What it pays. Roughly Rs 300 to Rs 2,000 an order, with festival hampers priced higher and usually ordered in batches. Best for anyone whose baking already gets requested at family events. 23. Event and wedding services Decoration, catering support, coordination and hosting, priced per event. Where to start. Local event planners who need reliable hands, and wedding marketplaces once you have photographs of your work. What it pays. Roughly Rs 3,000 to Rs 15,000 an event depending on the role and the scale. Best for organised people who stay calm under pressure and are free at weekends. 24. Selling on marketplaces Listing products on national platforms, with real reach and real competition. Where to start. Amazon Seller Central, Flipkart Seller Hub and Meesho. A GST registration is needed for most categories. What it pays. A margin per order after platform fees, shipping and returns, which is why unit economics matter more than volume in the first year. Unit economics decide this one. Best for people with a genuine product source, not for anyone hoping to arbitrage. 25. Interest and dividend income Fixed deposits, debt funds and dividend-paying stocks. It isn't exciting and it needs capital to matter, but it asks nothing of your evenings. Where to start. Your own bank for deposits, and a demat account for funds and shares. What it pays. A modest annual return on whatever is invested, which makes it the quiet third layer rather than a plan on its own. Best for people who already have savings sitting idle in a current account. Which Side Income Sources Work Alongside a Job? Working alongside a salaried job is normal, and there are three things to sort out before you start. Read your employment contract. Look for exclusivity, non-compete and outside-work clauses. Some employers require written permission, and asking first is a much easier conversation than explaining later. Keep it fully separate. Your own device, your own time, your own accounts. Never use office hours, office equipment or anything belonging to your employer. Plan for the tax. Side income is taxable. Keep a simple record of what came in and what you spent to earn it, and declare it when you file. Best fits for salaried people: financial product distribution, referrals, tutoring, freelance work in your professional skill, and asset rental. All of them run on evenings and weekends without a fixed schedule, and the first of them is explained in this guide to what a credit card agent does . One option, one month, then decide. That is the whole method. Which Side Income Sources Suit Students? Students have the two things that matter most here: time, and a network of people the same age. Start with what needs no capital. Tutoring juniors pays from the first week, freelance writing and design build a portfolio while paying, campus-level social media work for local businesses is usually uncontested, and financial product distribution becomes available once you turn 18. Skip anything that asks you to pay upfront for a kit, a course or a starter pack. Student-targeted schemes of that kind are common and none of them are side income. Best for building a skill and a track record at the same time, which is worth more at graduation than the money itself. Extra Income Sources Worth Avoiding Some categories look like side income and are not. Anything with a joining fee. No legitimate distribution or freelance platform charges you to start. Investment-first schemes promising fixed daily returns. That is not a side income source, it is a risk to your savings. Chain recruitment programmes where the money comes from signing people up rather than from selling anything. Survey and task apps as a main plan. They genuinely pay, but the amounts are small and the ceiling is fixed. Anything needing your OTP, password or documents shared with a stranger. If it takes money from you before it pays you, it is not income. What You Can Realistically Earn Nobody can promise you a number, and anyone who does is selling something. What can be said is how the shapes differ. Hourly work pays predictably and stops when you stop. Commission work pays nothing in a bad month and pays properly in a good one. Asset income is small but needs almost no attention once it is running. The realistic plan for most people is one of each: something predictable for the base, something with a ceiling for the upside, and an asset quietly earning in the background. Starting all three at once is the most common way to end up with none of them. Frequently Asked Questions What is the best side income source in India? The one that fits your time and skills, which for most people is either a skill they can freelance or a product they can distribute. Financial product distribution pays the most per hour spent because commission is paid per approved application rather than per hour worked. Which side income sources need zero investment? Financial product distribution, referrals, freelancing, tutoring, content creation, transcription and virtual assistant work all start with nothing but a phone or a laptop. Anything asking for a joining fee or a starter kit should be avoided. Can I do a side income with a full-time job? Usually yes, and many people do. Check your employment contract for exclusivity or outside-work clauses first, keep the work entirely separate from your employer's time and equipment, and declare the income when you file your taxes. What are good side income sources for students? Tutoring, freelance writing and design, campus social media work for local businesses, transcription, and financial product distribution once you turn 18. All of them need time rather than capital. How quickly can a side income start paying? Freelance and gig work pays within days of the first job. Commission-based work pays once an application is approved, usually within a week or two. Content-based routes such as blogging and YouTube take months before they pay anything at all. Is side income taxable in India? Yes. Income earned outside your salary is taxable, and it should be declared when you file your return. Keep a simple record of receipts and expenses from the day you start. Conclusion Twenty-five options is a menu, not a plan. The useful move is to pick one that matches your evenings and your existing skill, and give it a real month before judging it. If your network already trusts you with money questions, financial product distribution has the highest ceiling of anything on this list and costs nothing to try. If you would rather sell a skill than a product, freelancing pays sooner and more predictably. Either way, the first month is about learning what works, and the second is where the money starts. The rest of the partner journey is laid out in this guide to earning from home as a GroMo Partner . Disclaimer Nothing here is a guarantee of income. Earnings from every source listed depend on effort, demand, skill and, for commission-based work, approvals by banks and NBFCs. The ranges given for each source are typical market rates seen in India in 2026 and are offered as a guide only. They vary widely by city, experience, season and platform, and many people earn below the lower end while they are learning. Commissions are set by product partners and revised as campaigns change, so a figure that is accurate today can be different next month. Every GroMo commission quoted here is a maximum rather than a flat fee, is indicative only, and was read from the app on 12 August 2026 (GroMo product catalogue, retrieved 2026-08-12). Everything above is general information, not financial, tax or legal advice. Side income is taxable in India and should be declared. Read your employment contract before taking up outside work, and check the live commission in the GroMo app before quoting anything to anyone. Third-party platforms named in this article are mentioned for reference only and have no association with GroMo.

title: Lineage projects highlight sustainable transportation solutions in the cold chain
summary: Lineage is advancing sustainable transportation through electric yard trucks, renewable fuels, rail freight and supply chain optimization to help reduce cold chain emissions.
body_text: Blog // Services Lineage projects highlight sustainable transportation solutions in the cold chain August 07, 2026 Share This Article Facebook LinkedIn Twitter Collaboration is fueling sustainability progress in Seattle, where a Lineage facility recently replaced an older-model diesel yard truck with a new electric yard truck – an upgrade made possible with help from the Puget Sound Clean Air Agency , which partnered with Lineage to secure an Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) grant to fund the project. Through its Diesel Reduction Program , the Puget Sound Clean Air Agency partners with fleets to make the switch from diesel to zero-emission alternatives, bringing cleaner air to the region. Yard trucks (sometimes called yard goats) are on-premise vehicles used to move trailers from trucks to loading docks at a warehouse. Because they consume diesel fuel, traditional yard trucks have historically been contributors to Lineage’s total carbon emissions. The Orange EV yard truck, by contrast, does not generate emissions and has the added benefit of running quieter than their diesel counterparts. The new electric yard truck is an Orange EV model e-TRIEVER® which is a purpose-built, zero-emission Class 8 terminal truck. By transitioning to an electric yard truck, the facility is expected to reduce carbon dioxide, diesel particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and other pollutants emitted by diesel combustion engines. EV yard trucks also provide a better driver experience as they do not have the harsh vibration, engine heat, and noxious fuels that come with diesel engines. To date, Lineage has deployed more than 30 electric, zero emission yard trucks at facilities across our North American network. The transition to electric yard trucks, combined with our work to make our unloading schedules more efficient, is helping to reduce average emissions generated during this process. As part of the grant requirements, the retired diesel truck has been scrapped through a local recycling company. Piloting programs and projects with positive results The electric yard truck upgrade in Seattle is one of the latest examples of Lineage's ongoing effort to reduce the environmental impact of our operations. Because transportation is a significant contributor to our global emissions, we’re actively exploring multiple ways to make more efficient use of the fuel resources at our disposal. For example, we’ve conducted a pilot with a retail customer to understand how operating our fleet with hydrotreated vegetable oil (HVO) – a renewable fuel produced from vegetable oils and fats – might impact performance and emissions. The testing included baseline data measurements and eight weeks of data gathered from HVO-powered operations over routes spanning approximately 12,240 miles. We attempted to control as many variables as possible during this process, utilizing the same driver and vehicle on each set route, while also capturing variable data points such as external temperature, time of day and payload – all of which impact consumption rates. The results of the pilot were promising and showed an average reduction of approximately 92% in CO2 emissions as well as a positive increase in fuel consumption (around 8%). Another example comes from our European team, who rethought how trailers can be moved with help from an innovative company. Recognizing the sustainability benefits of rail transportation, they’re working with a company that developed a loading technique that allows for any type of European-standard semi-trailer to be carried by trains on railways. Through this collaboration, our team has successfully transported some of our semi-trailers using the rail motorway from the south to the north of France, reducing both the number of trucks on the road and their associated emissions. In 2024, we completed a total of 261 journeys using this rail motorway and achieved a carbon footprint reduction of approximately 314.1 tons (314,133.8 kg).* Leveraging data insights for greater efficiency On average, cold chain customers spend approximately 25% of their refrigerated supply chain costs on cold storage while transportation costs are often much higher. Using our in-house data science capabilities, Lineage supports customers seeking to optimize their supply chains with supply chain engineering . By taking a closer look at the data – facility locations, transportation modes and routes, inventory levels and demand patterns, and more – we can address specific challenges. One network insight analysis found a $2 million potential savings in transportation costs for a U.S. importer and exporter. For customers shipping to retailer or foodservice locations, Lineage’s multi-vendor consolidation program (called Lineage Velocities) can provide another way to control transportation costs and reduce empty miles. Velocities combines shipments with other vendors shipping to similar locations and building efficient, high-match deliveries. The shared truckloads help customers control costs and reduce wasted fuel from partial loads while also meeting strict delivery requirements. Lineage is also working with a leader in transportation technology and market insights to enable the decarbonization of our transportation operations. This collaboration enables us to enhance visibility across our transportation network, identify strategic opportunities, deliver sustainable fuel solutions, manage costs and foster equitable partnerships with carriers. We have leveraged this partner’s data to set miles per gallon (MPG) expectations to encourage our carriers to enhance their fuel efficiency and align with our environmental goals. Our transportation team proactively reviews our highest-emission lanes – often those involving long distances or high volumes – to uncover optimization opportunities or alternative mode opportunities. By strategically awarding transportation contracts and re-evaluating underperforming lanes, we prioritize partnerships with carriers who share our focus on emissions reduction initiatives. Additionally, Lineage participates in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) SmartWay Transport Partnership and has been recognized by the U.S. Department of Energy for its energy-efficient practices. Working together to make a better cold chain As a leader in the temperature-controlled logistics industry, Lineage is dedicated to continually improving our operations and reducing our environmental footprint while providing essential services to customers. The project with Puget Sound Clean Air Agency and Orange EV is a great example of how we work towards this goal with the support of corporate, non-profit, and NGO leaders in sustainability. To learn more about Lineage and our work to create a better cold chain, please see our website . Footnotes: *Emissions were calculated by our rail partner using the GEI informational methodological guide for transport services prepared by AD EME. Share This Article Facebook LinkedIn Twitter

body_text: Chartink Alternative for Intraday Trading: Build, Backtest & Execute Signals with AlgoTest AlgoTest Aug 10, 2026 • 8 min read • indicators • Markdown Twitter / X Facebook LinkedIn WhatsApp Ask ChatGPT Ask Claude Ask Grok Copy link If you use a Chartink screener for intraday trading, you probably already have a set of conditions you look for before taking a trade. It could be: RSI crossing a certain level A moving average crossover A volume spike A price breakout A combination of multiple indicators You can create these conditions in a Chartink screener, scan stocks, and get alerts when your conditions are met. But what happens after you find the setup? You may want to know if the setup actually worked in the past. You may want to test different entry and exit rules. And once you are confident about the strategy, you may want to execute it without manually watching the market. This is where AlgoTest can offer a different workflow. With Signals AI, you can build your trading signal , visualize it, backtest it, forward test it, and execute it live from one platform. What Is Chartink Used For? Chartink is a stock screening and scanning platform that helps you find stocks based on technical and fundamental conditions. For example, you can create a scan to find stocks where: RSI is above 50 Price is above the 20 EMA Volume is higher than the recent average Price breaks above a previous high Multiple technical conditions occur together Instead of checking hundreds of stocks manually, you can define your conditions and let the screener find stocks that match them. This makes Chartink particularly useful when you want to narrow down the market and find potential intraday or swing trading setups. You can also create alerts for your screening conditions and receive notifications when stocks match them. How to Use a Chartink Screener for Intraday Trading A typical intraday screening workflow looks like this: Define the setup you want to trade. Convert it into technical conditions. Create the conditions in a Chartink screener. Scan for stocks that match. Set an alert for matching setups. Decide whether to take the trade. For example, you may want to find stocks where: Price is above the 20 EMA RSI is above 50 Volume is above its recent average Price breaks the previous high A Chartink screener can help you find stocks that meet these conditions. But screening only tells you that a stock matches your setup. It does not tell you whether the complete trading strategy works. To answer that, you need to test the trading logic behind the setup. The Limitation of a Stock Screener A screener can tell you that your conditions are currently being met. It does not necessarily tell you whether the complete trading strategy works. Once you have created your setup, you may still want answers to questions such as: How often did this setup generate trades? How many of those trades were profitable? What was the average return? What was the maximum drawdown? What stop loss worked best? What target worked best? Did the strategy work in different market conditions? What would have happened if you followed the setup on every signal? To answer these questions, you need to test the trading logic itself. This is where the workflow can move from screening to signal building and backtesting. Related: 5 Best Indicators for Intraday Trading From Stock Screening to Trading Signals If you already know the conditions you want to trade, you can turn those conditions into a trading signal. This is where AlgoTest Signals AI comes in. Instead of stopping at: Create conditions → Scan stocks → Find setup you can take the workflow further: Build signal → Visualize → Backtest → Forward test → Execute Signals AI lets you create signal logic using AI or build and edit the logic directly on the Signals AI Canvas. You can then see where your signals appear on the chart and check whether the logic is behaving as expected. Check out Signals AI documentation for a step by step walkthrough How to Build Intraday Trading Signals With AlgoTest Signals AI canvas You do not have to start by writing code. You can describe your trading idea in plain English and use the AI Agent to create the initial signal logic. For example: Create a NIFTY intraday signal when the 20 EMA crosses above the 50 EMA and RSI is above 50. Exit when the 20 EMA crosses below the 50 EMA. Signals AI can convert the instructions into signal logic that you can review and modify. You can build signals using conditions based on: Technical indicators Price Volume Indicator crossovers Indicator comparisons Logical conditions Time based conditions You can also combine multiple conditions to create more detailed trading setups. This gives you more control over the actual signal logic instead of simply looking for stocks that meet a predefined scan. Related: How to Automate ADX Indicator Strategy Without Coding Visualize Your Signals Before Backtesting Before you test your strategy, you want to make sure the signal is being generated where you expect it to. Signals AI lets you visualize your signals directly on the chart. For example, if your strategy generates a buy signal when the 20 EMA crosses above the 50 EMA, you can look at the chart and check where those signals appear. This can help you identify issues in your logic before you move to backtesting. It also makes it easier to understand how your conditions behave across different market periods. Related: EMA Indicator Strategy: How to Automate It Without Coding Backtest Your Trading Strategy Once your signal logic looks correct, you can test it against historical market data. This is an important step because a setup that looks good on a few recent charts may not work consistently over a larger period. With AlgoTest, you can connect your signal to a trading strategy and backtest it. You can evaluate metrics such as: Cumulative P&L Win rate Maximum drawdown Year wise performance Number of trades Individual trade results For example, suppose your intraday signal generated 200 trades over your selected historical period. You can use the backtest results to understand how that strategy performed instead of relying only on a few successful examples. A backtest does not guarantee future returns. Actual results can differ because of factors such as slippage, execution delays, liquidity, and live market conditions. Forward Test Before Going Live Backtesting tells you how your strategy performed on historical data. You may also want to see how it behaves with live market data before using real money. This is where forward testing can help. With AlgoTest , you can forward test (also known as paper trading) your Signals AI strategy using live market data without deploying real capital. You can use this stage to check: Whether signals are generated as expected How frequently the strategy trades How the strategy behaves during current market conditions Whether your execution rules work as expected This gives you another layer of validation before live deployment. Popular: 7 Bollinger Bands Strategies for Indian Traders: Intraday, F&O and Swing Execute Your Signals Automatically Once you have built and tested your strategy, you can move to live execution through a connected broker. Instead of manually watching for every signal and placing an order yourself, you can configure the strategy to execute according to your predefined rules. Your workflow becomes: Signal condition is met ↓ Trading signal is generated ↓ Strategy executes according to your settings This takes you from identifying potential trades to running a defined trading process. Chartink vs AlgoTest for Intraday Trading Chartink and AlgoTest can serve different needs. If your main requirement is to screen stocks based on technical conditions, Chartink can be useful. title: FTC Solar Announces Second Quarter 2026 Financial Results
summary: Second Quarter Highlights and Recent Developments Second quarter revenue up 52% q/q, 31% y/y, ahead of target Awarded 400MW project with top EPC and top developer Awarded 80+MW project in Australia for 2H delivery Scheduled to begin deliveries on 330+MW Australia project Announced entry into India
body_text: Second Quarter Highlights and Recent Developments Second quarter revenue up 52% q/q, 31% y/y, ahead of target Awarded 400MW project with top EPC and top developer Awarded 80+MW project in Australia for 2H delivery Scheduled to begin deliveries on 330+MW Australia project Announced entry into India market with multiple initial project wins Reaffirm outlook for 40% y/y revenue growth in 2026 Announced agreement for up to $20 million equity line of credit with institutional investor AUSTIN, Texas, Aug. 05, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- FTC Solar, Inc. (Nasdaq: FTCI), a leading provider of solar tracker systems, today announced financial results for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026. “We’re pleased to report that second quarter results were in line with or better than our targeted ranges,” said Anthony Carroll, President and CEO of FTC Solar, “and that we remain on track to outpace the market with 40% annual revenue growth in 2026. “While I am just over one quarter into my tenure as CEO, the company has done an incredible amount over the past two years to put the company in a great position to grow and scale. This includes developing and introducing a 1P tracker line that is regarded by customers as easier and faster to install and an engineering capability that is willing to go the extra mile and increasingly helps enable more power or less land grading through a more efficient design. “To build on that foundation and continue the momentum, we have been focused on five key areas. They include: Expanding top 10 customer base . Following great work to achieve qualification with top prospects, including 9 of the top 10 EPCs, the focus now is on converting these opportunities and expanding our customer base within this group. We have recently signed two projects associated with three top developers and EPCs and expect to add projects with two more by year-end. Making immediate bookings progress. With a significantly expanded overall customer base and improved access to bid opportunities, our focus is now on converting that stronger pipeline into bookings. We're investing in sales talent, AI-driven bidding capabilities, and international expansion, with meaningful momentum in Australia and new entry into India reinforcing the opportunity ahead. Ramping second half revenue. Following 52% sequential growth in the second quarter, we’re looking for another 24% growth in Q3 before accelerating again in Q4. We’re reaffirming our full-year 2026 growth outlook of 40%. While we will look to grow even faster, what is most important is systematic execution and layering on an increasing amount of projects to build sustainable future growth. Cost and breakeven optimization: Improving our cost structure and lowering our breakeven revenue level remain key priorities. Through targeted cost savings, greater use of AI and automation, and better monetization of the value we deliver to customers, we see meaningful opportunities to expand margins as the business grows. Robotics and AI : We believe robotics will be a major productivity driver for our customers, and we want to help lead that transition. We've already generated promising test and pilot results and expect to have these technologies operating on commercial projects with real-world data soon. “Overall, while we still have work to do and need to win much more business, I'm proud of what our team has accomplished and confident in where we're headed. We have the products, the partnerships, and the strategy to drive sustainable growth, and we'll continue earning trust through execution and customer focus. Our opportunity is great, our plan is clear, the path to profitability is there, and our second half revenue growth outlook is very strong.” Second Quarter Results Total second-quarter revenue was $26.2 million. This represents an increase of 51.5% compared to the prior quarter revenue and an increase of 30.8% compared to the year-ago quarter. GAAP gross loss was $2.2 million, or 8.5% of revenue, compared to gross loss of $1.2 million, or 7.1% of revenue, in the prior quarter. Non-GAAP gross loss was $1.3 million or 5.1% of revenue. This compares to Non-GAAP gross loss of $3.5 million in the prior-year period. The contracted portion of the company's backlog2 now stands at approximately $560 million. During the quarter, the company received a purchase order for its first 1P tracker system with a top U.S. developer, which has heretofore been a 2P customer. The project is just over 100 megawatts and located on the East Coast. The company is very pleased to expand its relationship with this developer. The company also received notice to begin production on a 330+ megawatt project in Queensland, Australia. FTC first announced the project award in March 2025 with tracker production at the time expected to begin in mid-2025. The project timeline has been revised and now finalized with notice to proceed issued during the second quarter. Tracker deliveries begin in the second half of 2026. The aggregate value of the project was added to the company’s backlog in 2025 and was reflected in the most recent backlog disclosed on May 5, 2026. The company also announced that it has recently entered the India market, and has already won multiple initial projects there, ranging from pilot to 100+ megawatt projects with large and well-known customers. Shipments in this region have been ongoing in 2026. Subsequent Events Subsequent to quarter end, the company received a new 400 megawatt purchase order for a 1P project being constructed by a top 5 U.S. EPC and a top 5 U.S. developer. The company has worked with this EPC on other projects recently and is pleased to see a nice-sized follow-on project. In addition to its financial results, the company announced that it has entered into a purchase agreement establishing an Equity Line of Credit (“ELOC”) with Lincoln Park Capital, a long-only institutional investor. Under the terms of the agreement and subject to certain conditions, FTC Solar has the right to sell, and Lincoln Park is obligated to purchase, up to $20 million worth of common shares at prices that are based on the market price at the time of each sale. FTC Solar, at its sole discretion, controls the timing and amount of all sales of shares associated with the ELOC. There are no upper limits to the price per share Lincoln Park may pay and Lincoln Park has agreed not to enter into or effect any direct or indirect short-selling or hedging of our common stock. There are no warrants, derivatives, or other share classes associated with this agreement. The company believes that this agreement will provide the company with an additional and flexible source of funding as may be appropriate. Outlook The company expects third quarter revenue to grow by roughly 24% relative to the second quarter, based on the midpoint of the guidance range. The company expects further sequential growth in the fourth quarter and continues to expect full-year revenue 2026 growth of 40% relative to 2025, outpacing the market.
